extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and experienced inventors studying U.S. infringement law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of U.S. patent-law rules governing when and where infringement occurs, who may be liable (including government and municipalities), and special rules about reissues, expiration, and manufacture for export. Focused on legal doctrines and case-law guidance for determining liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct acts of making, using, and selling are separate infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts of making, use, and sale are essentially distinct infringements and vary in their effect according to the patentee's method of enjoying his monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of damages and available relief depends on which acts occurred; making, use, and sale can each give rise to liability separately. (Illustrative cases: Ree Colgate v. Western Electric Mfg. Co.; Blake v. Greenwood Cemetery.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint and several liability for making and selling
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one party makes and another sells, they are liable jointly and severally for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the maker and the seller can be pursued for infringement damages and equitable relief (Jennings v. Dolan and related cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: No infringement prior to patent grant (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invasion of the patentee's right is impossible until the patent has been granted; the date of the patent is the earliest moment at which an infringement can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under U.S. law, acts done before issuance are not infringements; English courts have treated some pre-issue acts differently. Re-issues are treated as new patents and, for this purpose, acts before they are granted are not infringements. (See Lyon v. Donaldson; notes on English practice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissued patents treated as new; scope and retroactivity limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue is considered a new patent for determining infringement timing; acts performed before re-issue are not infringements of the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, whether a re-issue with broader claims reaches devices that did not infringe the original depends on how the original patent is measured (by description or claims) and relevant case law (Ives & Miller v. Hartford Spring & Axle Co.; Cammeyer v. Newton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement generally must occur within the patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, infringing acts must be committed before the patent term (or any extension) has expired; the exclusive rights terminate at expiration and vest in the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have limited equitable relief after expiration, but have recognized an exception (manufacture during the term with unlawful intent) and sometimes enjoin post-expiration sales of articles piratically made during the patent's life. (See doctrine and cases such as American Diamond Rock Boring Co. v. Sheldon; decisions cited regarding injunctions for goods made during term.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture during patent term for post-expiration sale can be actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing patented articles in quantity during the life of the patent with intent that they be sold or used after expiration is a fraud on the patentee's rights and may be treated as infringement; courts have restrained post-expiration sale of such goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law treats use and sale after expiration of articles made without authority while patent was in force as infringements, making parties liable similarly as if acts occurred during the patent term. Courts have sometimes ordered destruction or restrained sale of such piratically made articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple connected patents (machine/process/product) are distinct; one patent's expiry doesn't free related patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents on associated inventions (e.g., machine, process, product) are distinct; the expiration of one patent does not release the public to use inventions still protected by other patents in the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product cannot be made or enjoyed without motor/instrumentalities covered by other patents, the public must wait until those patents expire. Separate patents may live independently and be enforced irrespective of the death of associated patents (Kelleher v. Darling; discussion of acts of July 4, 1836 and March 8, 1839).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope: infringement only within United States and defined maritime reach
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent protects the invention throughout the United States and its territories; the area includes waters embracing U.S. shores and American vessels wherever they sail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making, using, or selling within this area is infringement; making within the U.S. for sale abroad can be infringement. Foreign vessels lawfully entering U.S. ports raise nuanced issues—use on foreign vessels in port may not be infringement (Brown v. Duchesne), but furnishing articles here for use on such vessels can create liability for the furnisher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture in U.S. for sale abroad can infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: Making an article within the United States for sale abroad is an act that can constitute infringement even if the ultimate sale occurs outside U.S. jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages for making and selling in the U.S. (and for export-related acts) may be substantial; the unlawful making here is harmful to the patentee even if the sale is abroad (Ketchum Harvester Co. v. Johnson Harvester Co.; related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government cannot use patented inventions without compensation; officials may be liable
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. government cannot appropriate or use a patented invention without just compensation; officers or contractors acting for the government can be responsible for infringement unless use is under a lawful eminent-domain-like taking in public emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where government takes inventions for public emergency or necessity, it may do so but must make compensation; remedies against the United States are typically pursued in the Court of Claims. Some decisions consider whether individual officials are personally liable when acting solely for government benefit (James v. Campbell and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal and public corporations liable for infringement by officers/agents benefitting the corporation
rubrics_metrics.description: A municipal corporation is responsible for acts of infringement performed by its officers and agents for its benefit; boards or departments acting as city instrumentalities can render the city liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability depends on whether the infringing acts were for the city's benefit and whether profits or savings accrued to the city. Instrumentalities that operate under city control and account to the city can make the city a proper party to an account. But a municipality is not automatically liable for infringement committed by an independent contractor on its public works nor for articles supplied by such a contractor that were produced by infringing processes; contracts do not shift liability to the contracting public body absent proof of intent or concert.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere possession/manufacture without intent may not be infringement; intent to use/sell matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere making of an invention is not ipso facto infringement; it becomes infringement when coupled with an intent that the invention shall be used or sold in violation of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intent element informs doctrines like restraint on manufacture for post-expiration sale; courts consider purpose and intent to determine whether manufacturing alone constituted an evasion of patentee's rights (discussion in McKay v. Dibert and other cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief and remedies may be shaped by equitable considerations and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may tailor relief (injunctions, accounts, destruction orders) based on timing of acts, whether goods were made during patent term, and whether continuing sales would unfairly deprive patentee of benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include injunctions to restrain sale of piratically made goods even after patent expiration, and accounting for profits accrued to public bodies. The availability and scope of relief depend on case-law balancing of equities (cases and Chancellor Lyndhurst's statements referenced).
